prompt: What does a tutorial followed to the letter prove?

choices.text: That you choose good problems to work on
That you handle errors nobody warned you about
That you follow instructions carefully
choices.why: Right, and everybody else can show it too.

choices.text: That you design a system's structure from scratch

prompt: In a tutorial, which of these did somebody else decide? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The problem
The libraries
The steps that avoid the errors
Making it run on your machine
choices.why: That part is left to you.

prompt: A reviewer recognises a well-known tutorial from its file names. What happens next, by the lesson?
hint: It does not count against you.

choices.text: They read nothing else in it, and it simply does not count
They reject the application for copying code
choices.why: It does not count against you.

choices.text: They run it to see whether it still works
They compare it line by line with the original

prompt: The question to ask of anything in a portfolio: what did I ___ here that the instructions did not?
Which are on the lesson's definition of finished? Choose all that apply.
hint: Five things a reader can check.

choices.text: It runs from its README on somebody else's machine
It tests the rule most likely to break
It writes down two or three decisions
It uses a cloud provider's managed database

prompt: Why does the README have to work on somebody else's machine, and not yours?

choices.text: Yours is slower than the reviewer's computer
Reviewers are not allowed to use your laptop
A README is read on a phone, never on a computer
On yours everything is already installed
choices.why: Right. Lesson 16 tests it on a clean machine.

prompt: There is one file in the project you copied and could not rewrite. Is the project finished?

choices.text: Yes, if the file came from the official docs
choices.why: Where it came from is not the test.

choices.text: Yes, if the tests still pass with it
Not yet, since you could not explain every part
Yes, as long as the README credits the source
choices.why: Credit is honest, and still not finished.

prompt: In the figure, what does a reviewer count?

choices.text: Ticks, so five tutorials score higher
Lines ticked, not the number of ticks
The number of repositories on the profile
The number of features in each project
choices.why: Features are not on the list.

prompt: Match each part of finished to the lesson that deals with it.

pairs.left: It runs from its README elsewhere

prompt: What is depth, by the lesson?

choices.text: The number of features the project ships with
The point where something got hard and the author decided what to do
The number of lines in the largest file of code
How many languages the repository uses at once

prompt: In the git log capture, where is the oldest of the five commits?
hint: git log lists the newest first.

choices.text: At the top
In the middle
It is not shown
At the bottom

prompt: What does commit 2fb7c61's message do? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Names a failure that really happened
Says where the refusal lives, and why there
Ties the change to an issue
Lists every file of the project

prompt: Why does loanbook put the one-loan rule in the database rather than in a Python check?

choices.text: Python is slower than SQL at comparing two values
SQLite forbids any check written in application code
choices.why: It forbids nothing of the kind.

choices.text: It still refuses when two requests arrive together
choices.why: Right. A Python check reads available twice.

choices.text: The tutorial it came from did it that way

prompt: Put the three moves in the order the lesson gives them.
items: Change the problem, not the paint
Add the rule the tutorial did not have
Take it somewhere the tutorial did not go

prompt: Which change still leaves you with the same tutorial?

choices.text: A new colour scheme and a new name
A new problem with rules of its own
choices.why: That one changes everything below it.

choices.text: A rule the tutorial did not have
choices.why: That is code nobody wrote for you.

choices.text: A deploy the tutorial left as an exercise
choices.why: That goes where it did not.

prompt: What does the lesson say about naming the tutorial a project started from?

choices.text: Say it in the README; leaving it out is the weakness
Leave it out, since it makes the project look smaller
Mention it in the interview, never in writing
choices.why: The lesson puts it in the README.

choices.text: Rename the files so nobody can tell
choices.why: That is presenting it as yours.

prompt: What does the lesson suggest for tutorials you already have? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Leave them public and unpinned
Describe each in one line as a tutorial
Archive the ones you will not touch again
Delete them before applying anywhere

prompt: What does an archived repository tell a reader?

choices.text: It passed every item of the finished checklist
It was deleted and can no longer be opened
It is the project the author wants read first
It is left, read-only, not finished in lesson 2's sense

prompt: A candidate's weather app follows a popular tutorial, and they add a rule: warn when a saved city has not been refreshed in a day. Which move is that?
hint: A refusal, a limit, a date.

choices.text: Changing the paint, since it is the same app
Adding the rule the tutorial did not have
Taking it somewhere the tutorial did not go
choices.why: That would be deploy, accessibility, bad input.

choices.text: Nothing yet, since the problem is unchanged
choices.why: A new rule is code nobody wrote for you.

prompt: Five tutorials each run from their README. One project meets all five points of finished. What is the difference a reviewer sees?

choices.text: An address, tests, decisions and an explanation
choices.why: Right. The four lines the tutorials leave blank.

choices.text: None, since each one runs from its README
choices.why: That is only the first line.

choices.text: The tutorials win, because five is more than one
The project wins because it is larger
